title: Photoelectric emission from a metal
stem: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 250 nm falls on a clean metal surface whose work function is 2.3 eV. h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy of one photon, in eV.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the stopping potential needed to prevent all photoelectrons reaching the collector.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the threshold wavelength for this metal.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The intensity of the ultraviolet light is doubled. Explain, using the photon model, the effect on the photoelectric current and on the stopping potential.
markscheme: doubling intensity doubles the number of photons per second (same photon energy)
so (about) twice as many electrons emitted per second / current doubles
each electron still receives one photon of the same energy hf
so maximum kinetic energy and stopping potential are unchanged

title: Binding energy of helium-4
stem: The table gives masses of particles involved in the formation of a helium-4 nucleus. 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass defect of the helium-4 nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the binding energy per nucleon of helium-4, in MeV.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium releases energy in the core of a star.
markscheme: helium-4 has a much higher binding energy per nucleon than hydrogen nuclei
so the products have less total mass than the reactants / there is a mass decrease
the mass difference is released as energy according to E = Δmc² (kinetic energy of products / photons)
high core temperature lets nuclei overcome electrostatic repulsion so fusion can occur
